content.title: About
content.content: Pork ham hocks (smoked) are cuts from the front leg of a pig, usually with the bone attached, that undergo curing and smoking. They have a rich aroma, firm texture, and a slightly sweet, smoky flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ham hocks are a staple in traditional Russian dishes such as rassolnik and hearty broths.
Smoking preserves the meat by reducing moisture and creating antimicrobial compounds.
In many regions the hocks are served cold, thinly sliced as an appetizer.
High collagen content makes them a good source of gelatin when slow‑cooked.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Ham hocks provide high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which helps prevent anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, B6 and niacin, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides zinc and phosphorus, supporting immune health and bone strength.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Smoked hocks are often heavily salted, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: Smoking may introduce nitrite compounds, which are considered potentially harmful in large amounts.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Ham hocks contain saturated fats; people with high cholesterol should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the hocks thinly for cold platters, add them to soups, stews, or braise with vegetables. Before cooking, trim excess fat and rinse to reduce excess salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the hocks refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C in an airtight package for 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where they retain quality for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration, which indicate spoilage.
